passage:
Suraj: Did the whole monthly report again. Rohit sir left at five.
Suraj: Full-time staff, full salary. Me, free. 😠
Wasim: Ugh. Have you told your manager?
Suraj: No. Last week I "forgot" to send Rohit sir's file. Felt good for a minute, then awful.
Wasim: That backfires on you, not on him. What do you actually want?
Suraj: Clear scope. Someone to say what's mine and what isn't. And a good reference at the end.
Wasim: Then ask for exactly that.
Suraj: True. I have learned real reporting tools here. Doesn't mean every job is like this.
Wasim: Write it down and I'll read it first.
Suraj: Okay. Thanks 🙂

qa.q: When did Rohit sir leave, according to Suraj?
qa.a: Rohit sir left at five.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel after "forgetting" to send Rohit sir's file?
qa.a: He felt good for a minute, but then awful. It shows his resentment was strong, though quiet spite left him uncomfortable with himself.

qa.q: What could Suraj ask his manager for?
qa.a: He can ask for a clear list of what is his and what is not, and for a good reference at the end, and keep using what he is learning. 🙂

qa.q: How does Wasim see the "forgetting" of the file?
qa.a: Wasim thinks it would backfire on Suraj, not on Rohit sir, and steers Suraj back to what he really wants.

grounding: An intern covers staff work for free and seethes, then names the unfairness and decides to negotiate scope rather than sabotage.

passage: By eight every evening, the fifth floor of the startup was mostly empty, apart from the interns. Pallavi glanced at Uday's screen: he was still on the slides for a review that was not his job. "Send me the last three; I'll finish the charts," she said. Tomorrow he would do the same for her. They also traded tips: which meeting rooms were quiet, which senior answered questions patiently, how to say no to a Sunday call. On Friday Uday said, "All of us are working past eight. Maybe we should say so." They wrote a short, polite note together, with six names on it, asking about working hours and stipend timing. The manager read it twice. "Let's talk on Monday," she said. Pallavi's knees felt shaky, but she wasn't alone.

qa.q: What time was the fifth floor mostly empty every evening?
qa.a: It was mostly empty by eight every evening, apart from the interns.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi's knees feel shaky when the manager said "Let's talk on Monday"?
qa.a: She was nervous about how the manager might react to a complaint, but she felt steadier because six interns had signed together.

qa.q: What could the interns do before Monday's meeting?
qa.a: They can agree on the points they will raise, such as hours and stipend timing, keep their tone polite, and keep supporting each other instead of competing.

qa.q: How might the manager see the interns' note?
qa.a: The manager read it twice, so it clearly got attention. Six names suggest a shared concern rather than one person's grumble, and the reply was to invite a talk.

grounding: Interns cover for each other, share tips and together raise concerns about hours and pay.

passage:
"Uday, when Chacha comes tomorrow, tell him about your firm," Papa said, folding the newspaper. "Big name, no? I already told everyone."
Uday put his fork down. "Papa, I need to tell you something about the internship."
"Say."
"I'm not on the payroll. I'm an intern. Mostly I help with data entry and reports. It's not a salary job. I didn't correct you because you were so happy."
Papa was quiet for a while. "I told them because I was proud."
"I know. I'm proud too. I'm learning spreadsheets and how meetings work. And I'm applying for junior roles next month."
Papa nodded slowly. "Then tomorrow I will say: my son is learning at a big firm."
"That's true," said Uday.

qa.q: What did Papa ask Uday to tell Chacha about?
qa.a: Papa asked Uday to tell Chacha about his firm.

qa.q: Why had Uday not corrected Papa earlier?
qa.a: He did not want to spoil Papa's happiness, and he felt a guilty gap between what Papa told others and his own experience.

qa.q: What could Uday do next to keep Papa comfortable with the truth?
qa.a: He can share what he is learning and his plan to apply for junior roles, and keep Papa updated so pride can rest on facts.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt hearing the truth?
qa.a: Papa was quiet for a while, so he may have felt surprised or a little embarrassed. His offer to say "learning at a big firm" shows he still takes pride in Uday.

grounding: A parent proudly tells relatives about the big firm while the intern feels a guilty gap; he tells the truth gently and shares his plan.

passage: Jyoti stared at her phone at the traffic signal. The rate for each trip had dropped again overnight, and a red banner said her ID was blocked "pending review". No number to call, no person to write to. She had a full petrol tank she had just paid for and an evening of rent-money worries. Rehana, a rider from the tea stall, found her sitting on the kerb. "Screenshot the message, all of it," Rehana said. "And join our workers' group. We compare rates and share what works." Jyoti photographed the screen, then opened a notebook and began writing her trips and the fuel she used. That night she also texted a neighbour about tutoring evenings. It did not fix the block, but she felt less like a small cog in something she could not see.

qa.q: What did the red banner on Jyoti's phone say?
qa.a: It said her ID was blocked "pending review".

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when she found no one to call?
qa.a: She felt powerless and worried, since the rate dropped and she could not reach a person. Sitting on the kerb suggests she was overwhelmed.

qa.q: What steps did Jyoti take that could help her?
qa.a: She took screenshots, opened a notebook to track trips and fuel, joined the idea of a workers' group, and looked for tutoring as other income.

qa.q: How might Rehana see Jyoti's situation?
qa.a: Rehana knows how these blocks feel from the riders' group and wants Jyoti to have evidence and support. She sees it as a shared problem, not Jyoti's fault. 🤍

grounding: A platform cuts rates and blocks the rider's ID with no human contact; she keeps screenshots, tracks earnings after fuel, and looks to a workers' group and other income.

passage: I am Pallavi, and I live on the third floor. Last Thursday I was at my door, watching a delivery rider, whose bag said Harsha, climb up to 3B. The man in 3B opened the door, looked at his watch and said loudly, "Three minutes late. Every time." He did not look at the rider. I could not tell what Harsha felt; his jaw was tight, but his voice stayed even. "Sorry for the wait, sir. Traffic near the flyover." He handed over the bag, said thank you, and the door shut. Harsha stood a moment on the landing, took a long breath, and tapped his phone, maybe to report it. I said, "That wasn't right." He gave me a small nod and went down.

qa.q: Which floor does Pallavi live on?
qa.a: Pallavi lives on the third floor.

qa.q: What does Harsha's tight jaw and even voice suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he may have been hurt or annoyed but was working to stay calm. Pallavi says she could not be sure what he felt.

qa.q: What could Harsha do after such an incident?
qa.a: He can use the app's report tools, keep his dignity, and remember that the customer's rudeness says more about the customer than about him.

qa.q: How does the man in 3B seem to see Harsha in that moment?
qa.a: He seems to see Harsha only as a late delivery, since he checked his watch and did not look at him. He shows no interest in Harsha as a person.

grounding: A customer scolds a rider for being three minutes late without eye contact; the rider stays calm and reports, seen through a neighbour's eyes.

passage: The afternoon in Istanbul was hot enough to melt the asphalt, and Leila's bicycle basket bumped over the cobbles. Her last three customers had barely said hello, and one had slammed the door. At an old building near the tram stop, Elif answered in a floral housecoat. She looked at Leila's face, disappeared for a moment, and returned with a glass of cold water. "Drink. And take care on the road." Leila drank it all standing on the step. Something in her chest loosened. "Thank you," she said, and meant it. At the next street she saw another courier wiping his forehead by a fountain and pointed. "The tap works, it's cold." She did not let the slammed door decide her mood, nor let one glass of water make her think everyone was kind. But the day felt lighter.

qa.q: Where did Elif give Leila the glass of water?
qa.a: Elif gave it to her on the step of an old building near the tram stop.

qa.q: What does it mean that something in Leila's chest loosened?
qa.a: It means the small kindness relieved her tension after rude customers, and she felt seen and warmed by it.

qa.q: What could Leila do to keep her self-worth steady on hard days?
qa.a: She can accept kind moments warmly and pass them on, as she did, but not let a stranger's mood, kind or rude, decide her worth.

qa.q: How might Elif have seen Leila at the door?
qa.a: Elif looked at Leila's face and went for water, so she seemed to notice the heat and tiredness. To her it may have been a small, ordinary courtesy. 🙂

grounding: A customer offers water and says to take care on the road, a tiny kindness that lifts the courier's day; she accepts it and passes it on.

passage:
Dear Zainab,
I am writing this on the bus stop bench because I am too tired to call. For weeks I have stayed online eleven hours a day, chasing the bonus that is always one more trip away. Last night at a signal my eyes closed for a second and the horn behind me woke me. I sat with a notebook and finally worked out what I actually earn per hour after fuel. It is far less than I had imagined. I think the bonus is built to keep people like me hooked, and I fell for it. From Monday I will stop at a fixed hour and rest. I do not know if the bonus will be lost. But I would rather be safe and honest with myself. Please tell me if I am being silly.
Rehana

qa.q: How many hours a day had Rehana stayed online?
qa.a: Rehana had stayed online eleven hours a day.

qa.q: What did Rehana feel after Rehana's eyes closed at the signal?
qa.a: Rehana felt frightened and worn out. That pushed Rehana to face how tired things had become and to calculate real earnings.

qa.q: What could Rehana do to stick to the plan of resting?
qa.a: Rehana can set a fixed stopping hour, keep the notebook of hourly earnings, and talk with Zainab or other riders when the bonus tempts Rehana.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel reading Rehana's letter?
qa.a: Zainab may feel worried about Rehana's tiredness but glad to be trusted. Rehana asks whether that is silly, so Zainab can reassure Rehana that resting is sensible.

grounding: The rider chases incentive targets for eleven hours a day, then calculates the real hourly earnings and decides to rest.

passage: I am Farhan, and I still think about the day my bike chain snapped near the flyover. It was raining, I was already late, and a customer was calling every minute. I sat on the kerb feeling like the smallest person in the city. Then Naveen from the tea stall arrived with a spanner, and two others held an umbrella over my bag. That tea stall is where riders swap which lanes flood, which gates have rude guards, and who has spare parts. I feel like I belong there. Last month, after a week of long waits at restaurants, several of us wrote a short message to the platform asking for a fair waiting rule. No answer yet. But we wrote it together, and it felt good.

qa.q: Who arrived with a spanner when Farhan's chain snapped?
qa.a: Naveen from the tea stall arrived with a spanner.

qa.q: Why did Farhan feel like the smallest person in the city on the kerb?
qa.a: Farhan was alone in the rain, already late, with a broken bike and a customer calling every minute, so Farhan felt helpless.

qa.q: How could Farhan and the other riders use their network to improve their terms?
qa.a: They can keep sharing information, keep writing joint messages about waiting rules, and keep building trust so they speak together.

qa.q: How might Naveen see helping Farhan?
qa.a: Naveen probably sees it as normal among riders, since the group shares parts, routes and warnings. It shows the network works because people show up for each other.

grounding: Riders at the tea stall share routes and help with a broken bike, giving belonging, and use the network to ask for better terms together.

passage: Sunday night. Housewarming at Vijay Mama's flat, and I could not wait to leave. He asked, in front of everyone, "So, Preeti, what work are you doing now?" I heard myself say, "Logistics." My aunt nodded, impressed. I said nothing else, my face burning. The truth is I deliver food from seven to midnight, saving for my exam course, and I like the freedom. But in that room it felt like something to hide. Sitting on the bus home, I wondered what I was ashamed of. It is honest work. Next time, I will tell Mama plainly: I deliver food now, I am saving for my course, and I plan to change by next March. Lying makes me feel smaller than the job does.

qa.q: What work did Preeti tell Vijay Mama she was doing?
qa.a: She said she did logistics.

qa.q: Why did Preeti's face burn at the housewarming?
qa.a: She felt a private sting of shame because her relatives see delivery work as low status, and she had not told them the truth.

qa.q: What could Preeti say to her relatives next time?
qa.a: She can say plainly that she delivers food, is saving for her exam course, and plans to move on by next March.

qa.q: How might Vijay Mama react when Preeti tells him the truth?
qa.a: He may be surprised, and may or may not approve at first, since relatives see the work as low status. A clear plan and timeline may help him understand she is being serious.

grounding: The protagonist hides that she delivers food because relatives see it as low status, then decides to state it honestly with her plan.

passage: Thursday, late. Sunaina ma'am called at four to say the offer letter was coming by email. I said thank you, thank you, and my mouth stayed shut when I wanted to ask about the salary. My throat felt tight. What if they say, fine, we'll take someone else? Tonight I sat down with my notes. I read what people in similar roles usually earn and asked a senior from college what is reasonable. It turns out my offer is at the lower end. Tomorrow morning I will write to her: "Thank you for the offer, I am very excited. Based on my research and my skills, could we discuss a slightly higher figure?" If she says no, I will decide then. Silence would leave me resenting it for years. Nandini

qa.q: When did Sunaina call Nandini?
qa.a: Sunaina called at four.

qa.q: Why did Nandini's mouth stay shut on the phone?
qa.a: She was afraid that asking for more might make them withdraw the offer, and her throat felt tight.

qa.q: What could Nandini do if Sunaina says no to a higher figure?
qa.a: She can thank Sunaina, weigh the offer honestly against her needs and other options, and then decide calmly.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see a polite request from Nandini?
qa.a: Sunaina may see it as a normal, reasoned question from someone who is excited about the job. The tone and preparation make it easier to discuss.

grounding: The protagonist fears that asking for more will make them withdraw the offer, and plans a polite reasoned request rather than silently accepting.
